Soyez le bienvenu, M. le Président ! Vive M. Raymond Poincaré ! Or, in other words: Hurrah for the French President ! Welcome to London.
To-day M. Poincaré arrives in London on his long-expected visit, and London is prepared to welcome him as only London can.

In the streets that the French President will pass through during his three days' stay flags and flowery and kannettes have been hung with a lavish hand, metropolis should be as gay as the President's own Paris.

"Tutoyons" is the one word emblazoned on one of the banners that hang conspicuous over the City streets—" Let us call each other thing," in the French idiom; "Let's be pals" in the English. That is the spirit of the welcome London extends to Paris, the people of London to the President of the French Republic.

Already for the past two days London has become Gallicised partly by the incursion of French visitors, partly by the universal desire to know how to pronounce the word "Poincaré," difficult enough for English mouths, partly by the attempts to interpret the French legends on the banners in the City.
Londoners will have plenty of opportunities of seeing M. Poincaré during his stay, for the President will be about the town practically every hour of the day. (Photographs on page 1.)
MET BY THE PRINCE.
The Prince of Wales, with others of the party to receive the French President at Portsmouth, will leave Victoria at nine o'clock this morning on his first official mission.
His Royal Highness will be received with full naval honours, a salute being fired as his standard is hoisted on the semaphore tower in the dockyard.
While awaiting the President's arrival the Prince will lunch with Admiral, Sir Hedworth Meux and a party of naval and military officers at Admiralty House.
The French President, in the battleship Courbet, and the escorting squadron will reach Spithead at twelve o'clock, being received with a royal salute by the British fleet.

A new method of bringing sunken ships to the surface of the ocean, was demonstrated yesterday off Whitestone Landing, L.I. Jesse W.Reno, inventor of the escalator or moving stairway, is the inventor of the ship salvaging device. Hereof it has been impossible to salvage anything that had been submerged more than 60 feet. The invention of Mr. Reno include a cylindrical chamber, operated on tractor belts that enable it to chamber about the ocean bottom like a huge crab. The chamber is large enough for two men and contains its own oxygen and air filtering system, which enables the crew to live sixty-four hours under water. To the "crab" are fixed two steel drills which bore holes 5 inches in diameter in the side of the sunken vessels. Huge pontoons, like inverted water glasses are then hauled down by electricity to the tractor and large steel hooks on them are caught in the holes. The pontoons used yesterday had a lifting power of 100 tons each. The experiment was conducted on the sunken submarine chaser of the Eagle type used during the war, and accidentally sunk last December. In some way the pontoons broke away from the "crabs" and shot up through the water and into the air. Photo shows the pontoons on the surface of the water.

The Torpedoed Sussex. The cross-Channel steamer Sussex photographed lying in Boulogne Harbour showing the damage to her bows. At 80'clock on Friday March 24 a torpedo shattered the fore part of the vessel while she was making herway by an unusual course from Folkestone to Dieppo. There was some loss of life at the moment of the explosion. During the launching of the boats further loss followed and after 3 hours two of the boats capsized with more loss. About 100 persons are missing as a result of the attack.
